pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.1.1)
- B7.1.1.1 — Demonstrate understanding and the use of place value for expressing quantities recorded as base ten numerals as well as rounding these to given decimal places and significant figures.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- model number quantities of more than one billion using graph sheets, multi-base blocks and money
- compare and order whole numbers greater than 1,000,000,000 using >, < and =
- round whole numbers up, down and off to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand and hundred thousand
- round decimals to the nearest tenth, hundredth and thousandth
- express numbers to a given number of significant figures and decimal places

pages.title: Modelling numbers greater than one billion
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Model number quantities more than 1,000,000,000 using graph sheets, isometric papers and multi-base blocks.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.1
Our number system is a **base ten** (decimal) system. Each place is worth **ten times** the place on its right. In a numeral, the value of a digit depends on its **position** (place). This is called **place value**.
| **Billions** | **Hundred millions** | **Ten millions** | **Millions** | **Hundred thousands** | **Ten thousands** | **Thousands** | **Hundreds** | **Tens** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
The number in the table, followed by a 0 in the ones place, is **1,000,000,000 — one billion**. One billion is a thousand millions.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Place value** — The value of a digit is the digit multiplied by the value of its place. In 3,**7**45,000,000 the digit 7 is in the hundred-millions place, so its value is 7 × 100,000,000 = 700,000,000.
## ✏️ Example 1.1
Write 2,086,405,931 in a place value chart, in expanded form and in words.
**Solution**
| **B** | **HM** | **TM** | **M** | **HTh** | **TTh** | **Th** | **H** | **T** | **O** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0 | 8 | 6 | 4 | 0 | 5 | 9 | 3 | 1 |
Expanded form:
2,000,000,000 + 80,000,000 + 6,000,000 + 400,000 + 5,000 + 900 + 30 + 1
In words: **two billion, eighty-six million, four hundred and five thousand, nine hundred and thirty-one.**

pages.title: Modelling with multi-base blocks
pages.body:
## Modelling with multi-base blocks
In the classroom we cannot hold a billion objects, so we let one piece of a multi-base set stand for a large quantity. Suppose we agree that:
[[fig:m7-f02|Figure 1.1: Multi-base blocks used to model large numbers]]
| **Piece** | **Made of** | **Value it represents** |
|---|---|---|
| small cube | — | 100,000 |
| rod | 10 cubes | 1,000,000 (one million) |
| flat | 10 rods | 10,000,000 (ten million) |
| block | 10 flats | 100,000,000 (one hundred million) |
## ✏️ Example 1.2
How many blocks will make one billion?
**Solution**
One block stands for 100,000,000. One billion = 1,000,000,000.
1,000,000,000 ÷ 100,000,000 = 10
So **10 blocks** make one billion. (Ten blocks = 100 flats = 1,000 rods = 10,000 cubes.)
## ✏️ Example 1.3
Use the multi-base model above to represent 345,600,000.
**Solution**
345,600,000 = 300,000,000 + 40,000,000 + 5,000,000 + 600,000
300,000,000 → **3 blocks**
40,000,000 → **4 flats**
5,000,000 → **5 rods**
600,000 → **6 cubes**
## Representing a number in multiple ways
A number can be built from groups of 10s, 50s, 100s and 200s in many different ways — just like paying the same amount with different notes.
## ✏️ Example 1.4
Show two ways of writing 5,560 using multiples of 10, 50, 100 and 200 (use each figure at least once).
**Solution**
Way 1:
5,560 = 20 × 200 + 10 × 100 + 11 × 50 + 1 × 10
Check: 4,000 + 1,000 + 550 + 10 = 5,560 ✓
Way 2:
5,560 = 15 × 200 + 20 × 100 + 10 × 50 + 6 × 10
Check: 3,000 + 2,000 + 500 + 60 = 5,560 ✓

pages.title: Example 1.5
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 1.5
Using money tokens — GH₵20, GH₵50, GH₵100 and GH₵200 notes:
a) How many GH₵200 notes make GH₵185,000,000?
b) How many GH₵200 notes make GH₵1,890,750,000?
c) Find a combination of GH₵50, GH₵100 and GH₵200 notes that makes GH₵1,000,000, using every denomination.
**Solution**
a) 185,000,000 ÷ 200 = **925,000 notes**
b) 1,890,750,000 ÷ 200 = **9,453,750 notes**
c) One possible combination (there are many):
2,000 × GH₵200 = GH₵400,000
4,000 × GH₵100 = GH₵400,000
4,000 × GH₵50 = GH₵200,000
Total = GH₵400,000 + GH₵400,000 + GH₵200,000 = **GH₵1,000,000** ✓
> 🧪 **Activity 1.1 — Modelling one billion on graph sheets**
1. Each group takes a sheet of graph paper with 1 cm squares. Count the small squares in a 10 cm × 10 cm square (there are 100).
2. Let one small square represent 1,000,000. What does the 10 cm × 10 cm square represent? (100,000,000)
3. How many such big squares will represent 1,000,000,000? Shade them on graph sheets and display them on the class wall.
4. Use paper money tokens of GH₵20, GH₵50, GH₵100 and GH₵200 to model GH₵1,000,000 in at least three different ways. Compare your answers with other groups.
> ✨ **Did you know?** A stack of one billion GH₵1 coins would be several hundred kilometres high — taller than the distance from Accra to Kumasi! Large numbers are easier to understand when we model them.

pages.title: Comparing and ordering whole numbers
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Compare and order whole numbers more than 1,000,000,000 and represent the comparison using >, < or =.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.2
## Skip counting
Skip counting helps us see patterns in numbers. Counting forwards adds the same amount each time; counting backwards subtracts it.
## ✏️ Example 1.6
Skip count forwards and backwards from 1,000 in a) 25s b) 50s c) 250s. Give five numbers each way.
**Solution**
| **Count in** | **Forwards from 1,000** | **Backwards from 1,000** |
|---|---|---|
| 25s | 1,000, 1,025, 1,050, 1,075, 1,100 | 1,000, 975, 950, 925, 900 |
| 50s | 1,000, 1,050, 1,100, 1,150, 1,200 | 1,000, 950, 900, 850, 800 |
| 250s | 1,000, 1,250, 1,500, 1,750, 2,000 | 1,000, 750, 500, 250, 0 |
## More than and less than
## ✏️ Example 1.7
Find the number that is 500,000 more than, and 500,000 less than, 1,295,300,000.
**Solution**
1,295,300,000 + 500,000 = **1,295,800,000** (500,000 more)
1,295,300,000 − 500,000 = **1,294,800,000** (500,000 less)
So 1,295,800,000 is 500,000 more than 1,295,300,000, and 1,295,300,000 is 500,000 less than 1,295,800,000.
## Using the symbols >, < and =
> 🔑 **Key idea: Comparison symbols** — **>** means "is greater than", **<** means "is less than" and **=** means "is equal to". The symbol always opens towards the bigger number.

pages.title: Example 1.8
pages.body:
To compare two whole numbers:
1. Count the digits. The number with more digits is greater.
2. If they have the same number of digits, compare digits from the left (the highest place). The first place where the digits differ decides.
## ✏️ Example 1.8
Insert >, < or = to make each statement true.
a) 1,300,850,700 … 1,300,850,700
b) 5,223,487,637 … 5,113,487,637
c) 987,654,321 … 1,000,000,001
**Solution**
a) Every digit is the same, so 1,300,850,700 **=** 1,300,850,700.
b) Both have 10 digits. Billions: 5 = 5. Hundred millions: 2 > 1. So 5,223,487,637 **>** 5,113,487,637.
c) 987,654,321 has 9 digits; 1,000,000,001 has 10 digits. So 987,654,321 **<** 1,000,000,001.
## ✏️ Example 1.9
Arrange in ascending order: 2,045,300,000; 2,405,030,000; 2,045,030,000; 2,450,000,000.
**Solution**
All have 10 digits and begin with 2 billion. Compare the hundred millions: 0, 4, 0, 4. Then compare the ten millions and so on.
2,045,030,000 < 2,045,300,000 < 2,405,030,000 < 2,450,000,000
## Reading a number chart
## ✏️ Example 1.10
Study the number chart.
| 187,500 | 687,500 | 1,187,500 | 1,687,500 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,187,500 | 2,687,500 | 3,187,500 | 3,687,500 |
| 4,187,500 | 4,687,500 | 5,187,500 | 5,687,500 |
a) What is the rule for moving one step to the right?
b) Which number is on the right of 3,187,500? Write it in words.
c) What would be the next number after 5,687,500?
**Solution**
a) Each number is **500,000 more** than the number on its left.
b) 3,687,500 — **three million, six hundred and eighty-seven thousand, five hundred.**
c) 5,687,500 + 500,000 = **6,187,500**

pages.title: Rounding whole numbers
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Round (off, up, down) whole numbers more than 1,000,000,000 to the nearest hundred thousand, ten thousand, thousand, hundred and ten.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.3
We round numbers when an exact value is not needed — for example, "about 33 million people live in Ghana".
[[fig:m7-f03|Figure 1.2: 2,846,655 lies between 2,846,000 and 2,847,000]]
> 🔑 **Key idea: Round up, round down and round off** — **Round up**: always choose the larger of the two neighbouring values. **Round down**: always choose the smaller one. **Round off** (to the nearest): choose the value that is closer. If the digit after the rounding place is 5 or more, round off upwards; if it is 4 or less, keep the rounding digit.
## Steps for rounding off
1. Find the rounding place (e.g. thousands) and underline its digit.
2. Look at the digit immediately to its right.
3. If it is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, add 1 to the underlined digit. If it is 0–4, leave the underlined digit as it is.
4. Replace all digits to the right of the rounding place with zeros.
## ✏️ Example 1.11
Round 1,879,653 to a) the nearest hundred thousand b) the nearest ten thousand.
**Solution**
a) Hundred-thousands digit is 8; the next digit is 7 (≥ 5) → round up: **1,900,000**
b) Ten-thousands digit is 7; the next digit is 9 (≥ 5) → round up: **1,880,000**

pages.title: Example 1.12
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 1.12
Round 2,846,655 up, down and off to the nearest thousand, ten thousand and hundred thousand.
**Solution**
| **2,846,655 to the nearest …** | **Round up** | **Round down** | **Round off** |
|---|---|---|---|
| thousand | 2,847,000 | 2,846,000 | 2,847,000 |
| ten thousand | 2,850,000 | 2,840,000 | 2,850,000 |
| hundred thousand | 2,900,000 | 2,800,000 | 2,800,000 |
Notice: rounding off to the nearest hundred thousand gives 2,800,000 because the digit after 8 is 4 (less than 5), so 2,846,655 is closer to 2,800,000 than to 2,900,000.
## ✏️ Example 1.13
Round 4,375,962,518 off to the nearest a) ten b) hundred c) thousand d) ten thousand e) hundred thousand.
**Solution**
a) **4,375,962,520** b) **4,375,962,500** c) **4,375,963,000** d) **4,375,960,000** e) **4,376,000,000**
## Significant figures for whole numbers
> 🔑 **Key idea: Significant figures (s.f.)** — The significant figures of a number are its digits counted from the first non-zero digit on the left. To write a whole number to n significant figures, keep the first n digits (rounding the last one off) and fill the other places with zeros so that the size of the number does not change.
## ✏️ Example 1.14
Express 857,386,321 correct to a) five b) four c) three significant figures.
**Solution**
a) First five digits 85738|6… → the next digit 6 ≥ 5, so 85739 → **857,390,000**
b) First four digits 8573|8… → next digit 8 ≥ 5 → 8574 → **857,400,000**
c) First three digits 857|3… → next digit 3 < 5 → 857 → **857,000,000**

pages.title: Keep going
pages.body: > ⚠️ **Watch out!** When rounding a whole number to significant figures, never drop the zeros that hold the places. 857,386,321 to 3 s.f. is 857,000,000 — not 857!

pages.title: Rounding decimals
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Round decimals to the nearest tenth, hundredth, thousandth, etc.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.4
| **Ones** | **.** | **Tenths** | **Hundredths** | **Thousandths** | **Ten-thousandths** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | . | 3 | 6 | 8 | 5 |
The places after the decimal point are worth [[1/10]], [[1/100]], [[1/1000]], … We round decimals using exactly the same rule as whole numbers, but we **do not** add zeros after the rounding place — we simply drop the remaining digits.
## ✏️ Example 1.15
Round 486.3685 and 0.0605368 to the nearest tenth, hundredth and thousandth.
**Solution**
| **Number** | **Nearest tenth** | **Nearest hundredth** | **Nearest thousandth** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 486.3685 | 486.4 | 486.37 | 486.369 |
| 0.0605368 | 0.1 | 0.06 | 0.061 |
For example, 486.3685 to the nearest hundredth: the hundredths digit is 6; the next digit is 8 (≥ 5), so 6 becomes 7 → 486.37.
## ✏️ Example 1.16
Round 78.4604783 up, off and down to the nearest tenth, hundredth and thousandth.
**Solution**
| **78.4604783** | **Round up** | **Round off** | **Round down** |
|---|---|---|---|
| nearest tenth | 78.5 | 78.5 | 78.4 |
| nearest hundredth | 78.47 | 78.46 | 78.46 |
| nearest thousandth | 78.461 | 78.460 | 78.460 |
Note that 78.460 keeps its final zero: it tells the reader the number is correct to the nearest thousandth.

pages.title: Significant figures and decimal places
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Express decimal numerals to given significant and decimal places.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.5
> 🔑 **Key idea: Decimal places (d.p.)** — The number of decimal places is the number of digits after the decimal point. 745.97 has 2 decimal places.
**When is zero significant?**
| **Rule** | **Example** | **Significant figures** |
|---|---|---|
| Non-zero digits are always significant | 7.021 → 7, 2, 1 | count them |
| Zeros between non-zero digits are significant | 7.**0**21 | 4 s.f. |
| Zeros at the start of a decimal are NOT significant | 0.00234 → 2, 3, 4 | 3 s.f. |
| Zeros at the end of a decimal ARE significant | 0.36**0** | 3 s.f. |
## ✏️ Example 1.17
State the number of significant figures in a) 0.360 b) 7.021 c) 0.0045 d) 20.50
**Solution**
a) **3 s.f.** — the final zero shows accuracy to the thousandth.
b) **4 s.f.** — the zero lies between non-zero digits.
c) **2 s.f.** — leading zeros only fix the position of the point.
d) **4 s.f.** — 2, 0, 5, 0 are all significant.
## ✏️ Example 1.18
Round 0.00234567 and 84.40995000 to a) 3 s.f. b) 4 s.f. c) 6 s.f.
**Solution**
| **Number** | **3 s.f.** | **4 s.f.** | **6 s.f.** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00234567 | 0.00235 | 0.002346 | 0.00234567 |
| 84.40995000 | 84.4 | 84.41 | 84.4100 |
For 84.40995 to 6 s.f.: the first six significant digits are 8, 4, 4, 0, 9, 9 and the next digit is 5, so we round up: 84.4099**5** → 84.4100. The zeros are kept to show 6 s.f.

pages.title: Example 1.19
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 1.19
Express 745.9674 correct to a) three b) two c) one decimal place(s).
**Solution**
a) 745.967|4 → **745.967**
b) 745.96|74 → **745.97**
c) 745.9|674 → 9 + 1 = 10, so **746.0** (the zero must be written to show 1 d.p.)
## ✏️ Example 1.20
Musa measured the length of his teacher's table and wrote it correct to 2 decimal places as 0.76 m. State the possible actual readings he might have obtained.
**Solution**
Any measurement from 0.755 m up to (but not including) 0.765 m rounds to 0.76 m.
0.755 m ≤ actual length < 0.765 m
For example 0.755, 0.758, 0.761 or 0.7649 m.
> 🌍 **Maths in real life** Shopkeepers, pharmacists and engineers all round numbers. A pharmacist measures 2.5 ml of medicine (1 d.p.); a carpenter cuts wood to the nearest millimetre; Ghana's population is often reported to 2 or 3 significant figures.
> 💻 **ICT corner** Most calculators have a **FIX** mode (fixed decimal places) and a **SCI** mode (significant figures). Try setting FIX 2 and typing 745.9674 — the display shows 745.97.

questions.q: Investigate: Is 2.50 the same as 2.5? Explain the difference in what each number tells you.

parts.a: They have the same value, but 2.50 is given to 3 s.f. (accurate to the hundredth) while 2.5 is given to 2 s.f. (accurate to the tenth).

pages.title: Chapter 1 summary
pages.body:
- Each place in our number system is worth ten times the place on its right. One billion = 1,000,000,000.
- Compare whole numbers by counting digits, then by comparing digits from the left.
- Round **up** → larger value; round **down** → smaller value; round **off** → nearer value (5 or more goes up).
- Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros in decimals are not significant; trailing zeros in decimals are.
- Decimal places are counted after the decimal point.
